CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: China should announce retaliatory tariffs on the newly threatened US goods, matching the scale and scope of the US escalation. This signals resolve and preserves negotiating leverage without closing the door to future talks. Retaliation must be calibrated to hit politically sensitive US sectors (agriculture, automobiles) to create domestic pressure on the Trump administration.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat score of +0.45 reflects that the US has already imposed tariffs on $250 billion of Chinese goods (roughly half of US-China trade) and President Trump has threatened to tariff the remaining $267 billion, which would cover virtually 100% of bilateral trade (Fox Business/Motley Fool transcript). This represents a serious and escalating threat to China's export economy. However, the threat is not yet existential because: (1) China has already retaliated on $110 billion of $130 billion in US imports to China, demonstrating capacity to absorb and respond; (2) China's exports are part of global value chains where more than half the value comes from components sourced in other countries like South Korea and Japan, meaning US tariffs also hurt US firms operating in China (Brookings/Dollar); (3) China has strategically lowered tariffs on goods from other countries to redirect demand away from US products. The action score of -1.0 (retaliate) is justified because: (a) the US has escalated aggressively and China must demonstrate it will not 'cave in' (Brookings/Dollar notes it is 'unlikely that the Chinese leadership will cave'); (b) retaliation on agricultural goods and automobiles targets Trump's political base in the Midwest and South, creating domestic political costs; (c) China has already shown willingness to buy more US products and open markets, so its negotiating position is clear — but conceding now without retaliation would signal weakness and invite further escalation. The Fox Business article explicitly frames this as a war 'America must win,' confirming the US administration views this as zero-sum, which makes early concession strategically dangerous for China.
key_factors: US tariffs already cover $250B of Chinese imports (~50% of bilateral trade), with threat to cover remaining $267B
China has retaliated on $110B of $130B in US imports to China, nearly exhausting retaliatory capacity
US administration views trade war as zero-sum political strategy (Fox Business: 'one war America must win')
China's role in global value chains means US tariffs also damage US firms and third-country suppliers
Agricultural and auto tariffs target Trump's political base in Midwest and South
China has signaled willingness to negotiate but will not accept terms under duress
